corpus_scope: Overview only: PDF pages 35-73 (printed pages 1-39); see data/manifest.json
language: en (questions and answers in English to match the English corpus)
split_policy: Split fixed before any retrieval run: 15 dev / 5 test. Test gold pages (46, 58, 61, 67, 73) do not overlap any dev gold page. Single-document corpus, so topics (poverty, IDA, climate risk, emissions) recur across splits; leakage risk is recorded, not eliminated.
filter_policy: filter is a pre-retrieval input stated in the question context (the user names the Overview section). Values come from the page-level section mapping in data/manifest.json. Config C applies the filter only when filter is not null; otherwise it runs unfiltered.
evidence_verification: Each evidence_quote is a verbatim span of the pypdf 6.21.4 text of gold_page (NFC), compared after collapsing runs of whitespace (including line breaks) to a single space. Evidence is taken only from body text, not from figure/map labels or notes.

type_labels.condition: answer depends on a scenario, condition or qualifier
type_labels.metadata_filter: question context names an Overview section; the same topic appears in another section

questions.question: What share of the global population lives in extreme poverty in 2024, and how many people is that?
questions.expected_answer: About 8.5 percent of the global population, i.e. 692 million people living on less than $2.15 per person per day.
questions.evidence_quote: About 8.5 percent of the global population lives in extreme poverty in 2024. This means that 692 million people worldwide live on less than $2.15 per person per day

questions.question: Under a scenario where every country grows 2 percent per capita per year, how much faster would poverty be eradicated if each country's Gini index also fell by 2 percent annually?
questions.expected_answer: It would take 40 years less: 20 years instead of 60 years.
questions.evidence_quote: under the 2 percent per capita growth scenario, if the Gini index in every country were to also decrease by 2 percent annually, it would take 40 years less to eradicate poverty (20 versus 60 years).

questions.question: How much in potential lifetime earnings does the current generation of students risk losing, in present value?
questions.expected_answer: $21 trillion in potential lifetime earnings in present value, equivalent to 17 percent of today's global GDP.
questions.evidence_quote: This generation of students now risks losing $21 trillion in potential lifetime earnings in present value, or the equivalent of 17 percent of today’s global GDP

questions.question: In the Progress section of the overview, what share of the global extreme poor live in countries eligible for IDA support?
questions.expected_answer: IDA-eligible countries account for 7 in 10 of the global extreme poor.
questions.evidence_quote: countries eligible for support through the International Development Association (IDA) account for 7 in 10 of the global extreme poor.

questions.question: What is the Global Prosperity Gap and what prosperity standard does it use?
questions.expected_answer: It is the average factor by which incomes need to be multiplied to bring everyone in the world to the prosperity standard of $25 per person per day.
questions.evidence_quote: The Global Prosperity Gap is the World Bank’s new measure of shared prosperity (see box O.1). It is the average factor by which incomes need to be multiplied to bring everyone in the world to the prosperity standard of $25 per person per day
questions.review_note: Quote extended to include the sentence naming the Global Prosperity Gap (the original quote began with an unresolved 'It').

questions.question: At what annual rate did the Global Prosperity Gap improve between 1990 and 2024, and what drove it?
questions.expected_answer: 2.34 percent per year, with global mean income rising 1.48 percent per year and global inequality declining by 0.86 percent.
questions.evidence_quote: Between 1990 and 2024, the Global Prosperity Gap improved at an annual rate of 2.34 percent, with global mean income increasing at an annual rate of 1.48 percent and global inequality declining by 0.86 percent.

questions.question: What proportion of people worldwide face a high risk of a severe climate shock they would struggle to recover from?
questions.expected_answer: Nearly one in five people (17.9 percent).
questions.evidence_quote: Nearly one in five people (17.9 percent) is at high risk from climate-related hazards globally, meaning they are likely to experience a severe climate shock in their lifetime that they will struggle to recover from.

questions.question: In low-income countries, what share of natural disaster losses was covered by insurance?
questions.expected_answer: Less than 10 percent of losses were covered by insurance in low-income countries (compared with about one-third of the $380 billion global natural-disaster losses in 2023), forcing governments to redirect limited development funds toward disaster recovery.
questions.evidence_quote: In 2023, the estimated global economic losses due to natural disasters was $380 billion,15 of which only about one-third were covered by insurance. In low-income countries, less than 10 percent of losses were covered by insurance, forcing governments to redirect limited development funds toward disaster recovery.
questions.review_note: Quote extended to include the preceding sentence so 'losses' is tied to natural disasters. Quote contains the extraction artifact 'billion,15' (footnote 15), kept verbatim.

questions.question: How many people did Bangladesh evacuate for Cyclone Amphan in 2020, and how many fatalities were there?
questions.expected_answer: 2.4 million people were evacuated, with 20 fatalities.
questions.evidence_quote: in 2020, Bangladesh evacuated 2.4 million people for Cyclone Amphan, with 20 fatalities.

questions.question: Relative to 2019, how much additional emissions would eradicating extreme poverty entail, and how much would they reach at the $6.85-per-day poverty line?
questions.expected_answer: Eradicating extreme poverty would entail 4.7 percent more emissions than in 2019; at $6.85 per person per day, additional emissions would reach 46 percent (with historical emission intensities).
questions.evidence_quote: Eradicating extreme poverty would entail 4.7 percent more emissions than in 2019 (figure O.10). This number becomes larger at higher poverty lines. At $6.85 per person per day, additional emissions would reach 46 percent with historical emission intensities
questions.review_note: Question no longer equates extreme poverty with $2.15 (that link is not in this quote); answer limited to what the quote states.

questions.question: Why are cuts in coal production unlikely to hurt national employment much in a major coal exporter like Indonesia?
questions.expected_answer: Because the coal industry has a low labor share: in Indonesia it accounts for less than 2 percent of GDP and employs only 0.2 percent of the workforce.
questions.evidence_quote: Reductions in coal production are unlikely to have substantial effects on national employment and output in many economies because of the industry’s low labor share. For example, in Indonesia, the world’s second-largest coal exporter, the coal industry’s share of the GDP is less than 2 percent, and it employs only 0.2 percent of the workforce
questions.review_note: Quote extended to include the preceding sentence that states the reason (low labor share); the answer's 'low labor share' is now inside the evidence.

questions.question: How large have interest payments on external debt in IDA countries become?
questions.expected_answer: They have quadrupled since 2012, reaching an all-time high of $23.6 billion.
questions.evidence_quote: Interest payments on their total external debt stock in IDA countries have quadrupled since 2012, reaching an all-time high of $23.6 billion
questions.review_note: Gold page PDF 64 is a mixed-section page; this evidence starts after the 'Priorities:' heading, so section=priorities.

questions.question: In the Priorities section of the overview, what share of the global poor are current IDA countries projected to account for in 2030?
questions.expected_answer: 82 percent of the global poor in 2030 (and 90 percent of the global extreme poor in 2050), with currently projected growth rates.
questions.evidence_quote: Current IDA countries will comprise 82 percent of the global poor in 2030 with the currently projected growth rates, and 90 percent of the global extreme poor in 2050.

questions.question: What shares of global CO2 emissions and of the global population do high-income and upper-middle-income countries account for?
questions.expected_answer: High-income countries: 32 percent of global CO2 emissions and 15 percent of the population; upper-middle-income countries: 52 percent of emissions and 35 percent of the population.
questions.evidence_quote: High-income countries and upper-middle-income countries respectively account for 32 percent and 52 percent of global CO2 emissions, while accounting only for 15 percent and 35 percent of the global population.

questions.question: Which country is cited as an example of a country with significant renewable potential that can fully decarbonize its power system without higher costs?
questions.expected_answer: Brazil: countries with significant renewable potential, like Brazil, can fully decarbonize their power systems without higher costs or compromising resilience.
questions.evidence_quote: Recent evidence indicates that countries with significant renewable potential, like Brazil, can fully decarbonize their power systems without higher costs or compromising resilience
questions.review_note: Replaced 2026-11-14. Previous q15 (fossil primary energy to fall ~60% by 2035 / 90% by 2050) was dropped: the source sentence does not state whether the fall applies to high-income and upper-middle-income countries or globally. New question uses the same gold page; evidence states the answer directly.

questions.question: How has the count of high-inequality economies (Gini above 40) changed over the past decade?
questions.expected_answer: It fell from 66 economies a decade earlier to 49 in the most recent year.
questions.evidence_quote: The number of economies with high inequality has fallen, from 66 a decade earlier to 49 in the most recent year.

questions.question: How has the share of global emissions covered by carbon taxes and emission trading systems changed since 1990?
questions.expected_answer: It increased from 0.15 percent of global emissions in 1990 to 24 percent in 2024.
questions.evidence_quote: The coverage of carbon taxes and emission trading systems (ETS) has increased from 0.15 percent of global emissions in 1990 to 24 percent in 2024.

questions.question: In the Pathways section of the overview, what global health cost is attributed to air pollution?
questions.expected_answer: A global health cost equal to 6.1 percent of global GDP in 2019.
questions.evidence_quote: Air pollution today carries a global health cost representing 6.1 percent of global GDP in 2019

questions.question: In the Priorities section of the overview, what share of the population in IDA countries is exposed to extreme weather hazards, and what share is at risk?
questions.expected_answer: Of the IDA-country population covered by the report's extreme-weather risk data, 56 percent are exposed and 47 percent are at risk, so 84 percent of those exposed are also at risk.
questions.evidence_quote: For example, of the population in IDA countries covered by the data on risks from extreme weather events used for this report, 56 percent are exposed to extreme weather hazards and 47 percent are at risk. This means that 84 percent of those who are exposed are also at risk.
questions.review_note: Quote extended to include 'of the population in IDA countries covered by the data...' (original quote did not name IDA).

questions.question: If warming exceeds 2°C, how high could adaptation costs in Africa rise by the 2070s?
questions.expected_answer: Up to $200 billion per year by the 2070s (current adaptation costs in Africa are estimated at $7-$15 billion per year).
questions.evidence_quote: Current adaptation costs in Africa are estimated to be in the range of $7–$15 billion per year, with projections suggesting these could rise to $35 billion annually by the 2040s and up to $200 billion per year by the 2070s if warming exceeds 2°C.
questions.review_note: Replaced 2026-11-14. Previous q20 (costs could reach 7% of Africa's GDP by 2100 without adaptation) was dropped: the source says only 'costs' and does not state whether these are adaptation costs or climate damage costs. New question uses the same gold page; 'these' in the evidence refers to adaptation costs in Africa named in the same sentence. The answer does not use the $35 billion/2040s figure, because the source sentence does not make clear whether the 2°C condition also applies to it.

review_status_labels.assistant_checked: Assistant script found evidence_quote verbatim on gold_page (after whitespace collapse) and the assistant read expected_answer against the quote. Not an independent human verification.
review_status_labels.needs_learner_review: Evidence is verbatim on gold_page but whether it fully supports the answer is ambiguous; the learner must decide before freezing the benchmark.

section_check: Section is assigned from the evidence span, not the whole page. Only q12 has a gold page with two sections (PDF 64); its evidence lies after the Priorities heading. No question uses PDF 53 or the figure-only pages 37, 48, 50.
